paragraphs.text: 1. C. Valerius Flaccus, Argonautica, Book One.

I sing of the straits first opened to the great sons of gods,
and of the prophetic ship that dared to follow
the shores of Scythian Phasis and to burst through the midst
of the clashing crags, until at last it came to rest in flaming heaven.
Phoebus, instruct me, if the chaste tripod of the Cumaean seer
stands witness in my pure house, if the laurel grows green
worthy upon my brow; and you, to whom belongs the greater
fame of the opened deep, since the Caledonian Ocean
bore your sails, though once it scorned the Phrygian line of Iulus,
snatch me away from the peoples and from the earth wrapped in cloud,
holy father, and favour me as I sing the venerable
deeds of men of old. Your son shall unfold the overthrow of Idume
(for he is able): your brother black with the dust of Jerusalem,
hurling firebrands and raging through every tower.
He shall establish for you the worship of the gods and your nation's shrines,
when you, father, shall shine from every
quarter of the pole, and no longer shall the Bear be surer
to Tyrian keels, nor Helice be watched by Greek helmsmen,
but you shall give the signs, with you as guide shall Greece
and Sidon and the Nile send forth their ships. Now, serene,
favour my beginnings, that this voice may fill the Latin cities.

Pelias from his earliest years held Haemonia in his rein,
already a heavy and long-standing dread to his peoples: whatever rivers of his land
seek the Ionian Sea, and Othrys and Haemus,
and lowest Olympus too the fortunate man turned over with his ploughshare.
But there was no rest in his mind, fearing the offspring
of his brother and the threats of the gods; for the seers foretell
that this man will be the king's destruction, and at the altars
the terrifying warnings are repeated over the slain beasts: above all,
the man's own vast fame presses, and his prowess, no joy to a tyrant.
Therefore he goes on to forestall his fears and to destroy the youth,
the son of Aeson, and he turns over in his mind the ways and times of death.
But he sees no wars among the Greek cities, nor any
monsters: already Alcides has closed within his temple the jaws
of the Cleonaean lion; long since the Arcadian beast
was overcome by the serpent of Lerna, and both bulls had their horns broken.
The rage of the sea and the perils of the vast deep please him.
Then, looking on the youth with calm and no fearsome brow,
he accosts him, and gives his face and weight to feigned words.
'Grant me this campaign, fairer than the deeds of old,
and lend me your spirit. You have heard how Phrixus, of our blood,
the son of Cretheus, fled from his father's altars.
Him fierce Aeetes, who dwells in Scythia and by frozen Phasis
(alas, the shame of the great Sun), the wine of hospitality
. . .
mindful of nothing of ours or of the gods. Not rumour alone
reports it: the youth himself I see, lamenting such cruelty,
him I behold, when late sleep binds my weary limbs;
for his mangled shade with ceaseless complaints
rouses me, and Helle, the power of the great sea.
If I had the strength I once had, you would see the Colchian
already pay the penalty, and the king's head and arms here.
That fire has grown dull with the years, and my son is not yet
ripe for command and the business of war and of the sea.
You, in whom now both care and a man's spirit flourish,
go, my glory, and to the Greek dome restore the fleece
of Nephele's ram, and deem yourself worthy of such perils.'
With such words he urges the youth on, and, nearer than one who orders,
he fell silent, certain that the Cyanean rocks would clash
in the Scythian sea, and that the fleece, possessed by so great a serpent,
lay still—the serpent the king's daughter would call
from its shrine, flickering its forked tongues, with song and banquets,
and give it dark honey from her threefold venom.

Soon the silent guile lay open, nor was the fleece a care
to the man, but he saw himself driven by hatred onto the monstrous
seas. Yet by what art might he at last seek the bidden
Colchians? Now he longs for the winged sandals
of aerial Perseus, or burns to have curbed savage dragons
to a chariot, like the man who steeped in his plough the lands
that knew not Ceres, and condemned the oak by the golden corn-ear.
Alas, what is he to do? Should he summon the fickle people,
hostile to the old tyrant, and the fathers who once
pitied Aeson? Or, relying on Juno as ally and Pallas,
should he rather prevail by clashing arms and undertake the bidden seas,
if from so great a deed, the sea subdued, some
fame might arise? You alone, Glory, scorch the spirits and minds of men;
you he sees green and free from old age,
standing on the bank of Phasis and calling young men.
At last religion steadies his uncertain mind and his confused
breast, and stretching his pious palms to the stars
he says: 'Almighty queen, whom—when troubled Jupiter
shook the dark rain from a black sky—
I myself bore over the swollen Enipeus through the headlong storm
into the fields and to safety, nor could I believe
you a goddess, until I saw you reclaimed by your husband's
thunder and his nod, and snatched away in sudden fear,
grant me Scythia and Phasis; and you, unwed Pallas,
rescue me. To your temples I myself shall give
that fleece, and my father shall give to the fire necks
with gilded horns, and snowy flocks shall ring the altars.'

The goddesses heard, and with swift gliding through the air
they sought their separate ways. To the walls of Thespiae
the swift Tritonia flies, and to her dear Argus.
She bids him build the ship and bring down with the axe
the oak-trees, and now she goes as his companion into the Pelian shades.
But Juno, through the Argive and Macetian cities alike,
spreads word that the son of Aeson, untried, attempts
the south winds against his parents' wish; that already the ship stands ready, proud with its oars,
and demands men whom it may carry back and lift to glory through the ages for their deeds.

Every band of leaders longs—those already tested in war
and by fame—or those whom the trials of first youth
in its flower hold, with no chance yet of great deeds given:
but those who have a love of the fields and the harmless plough,
these the Fauns, seen in clear light, spur on, and sing
with great praise the ship through the wilds and the ways,
the goddesses of the woods and the river-gods with lifted horns.

At once, of his own will, from Inachian Argos the Tirynthian
hastens, whose darts, tipped with Arcadian venom,
and ready bow upon glad shoulders, the boy
Hylas carries: he indeed would wish it, but his hand was not yet
equal to the burden, nor could grasp the club. Frenzied with such things,
Saturnia pursues them and renews her wonted complaints:
'O would that not all the glory of Greek youth
were rushing into new dooms, and that these were now
the orders of my Eurystheus. The rain and darkness and the savage trident,
even now would I have hurled, and my husband's fire against his will.
Now too I would not wish him a comrade or the pillar
of our ship, nor may it ever be right to trust to Herculean
aid, or to owe so much to a proud companion.'
She spoke, and turned her eyes away to the Haemonian waters.
She sees all astir with a throng of men, and on every side
the felled grove brought down, and the shores resound
with the skilled axe; already she sees the Thespian's son
loosen the pine with a slender saw and join its side,
and soften the pliant timbers with slow fire, the oars now ready,
and Pallas seeking arms for the sail-bearing mast.
When the hull stood firm, a mass impassable to the long sea,
and when the thin wax filled the hidden
cracks, he added to the painting its various honours.
Here, on the back of a Tyrrhenian fish, longed-for . . .
Thetis is borne to the bridal chamber of Peleus; a dolphin
seizes the waters, she sits with her gaze cast down beneath her veil,
and sighs that no Achilles greater than Jove is to be born.
Panope and her sister Doto and Galatea, rejoicing in the wave,
attend her likewise with their gleaming arms,
seeking the deep: from the Sicilian shore the Cyclops calls her back.
Opposite, a fire and a couch of green foliage and feasts
and wine, and amid the sea-gods with his bride
the son of Aeacus, and Chiron strikes the lyre after the cups.
In another part is Pholoe, and Rhoetus mad with much wine,
and the sudden battles over the Atracian maiden.
The mixing-bowls fly and the tables and the altars of the gods
and the cups, the famed work of men of old. Best with the spear
here is Peleus, here Aeson is known raging with the sword;
on his unwilling back Monychus bears Nestor the victor,
Clanis dispatches Actor with a burning oak;
on his black horse Nessus flees, and leaning on the rugs
in their midst Hippasus hides his head in the empty gold.

Though these things were marvellous to the men, the son of Aeson is stunned,
and says to himself: 'Alas, wretched are our sons and fathers.
For this are we, easy souls, sent against the clouds
upon a ship? Shall the sea now rage on Aeson alone?
Shall I not carry off the youth Acastus into the same chances
and perils? Let Pelias wish safe waters for the hated keel
and entreat the waves, with our mothers, for it.'

As he hesitated over such things, the armour-bearer of Jove came
on the left through the air, and lifted up a lamb fixed in his strong talons.
But from afar, alarmed, the shepherds follow with shouting
from the stalls, and the barking of dogs; swiftly the raptor takes the air,
and escapes above the depths of the Aegean deep.
The son of Aeson accepts the augury, and glad seeks
the house of proud Pelias. Sooner now the royal son
flies to him, joining embraces and brotherly hearts.
The leader says: 'I come not, as you think, Acastus, with degenerate
complaints: my purpose is to join you as companion to my undertaking;
for neither Telamon nor Canthus nor Idas,
nor the son of Tyndareus, is worthier to me of Helle's fleece.
O how much of earth, how much of heaven it is permitted
us to know, to what uses we open the sea!
Now perhaps you think the toil grievous; but when the ship returns
glad and gives me back my dear Iolcos,
what shame, alas, will it be then for you to hear of our labours,
when I tell of the peoples seen, while you sigh.'

The king did not let the man say more: 'Enough have I prepared
for whatever you call me to; nor think us,' he said, 'best of men,
sluggish, nor that I trust my father's kingdoms
more than you, if under your lead it is settled to gather
the first honours of valour and to grow into a brother's fame.
Indeed, lest any care of my anxious parent hinder me
with excessive fear, I shall deceive him unknowing, and sudden
I shall be there with the ready crew, when the ship first leaves the sands.'
He had spoken. The other, glad, accepts these spirited promises,
and turns his eager steps to the shore.

But at the leader's commands and warning the Minyans in crowds
put their shoulders beneath the ship, and with bent knee bowed forward
run down and enter the strait. Neither the boatmen's
shout from panting chests was lacking, nor charming Orpheus with his shell.
Then glad they raise the altars. To you, ruler of the waters,
the highest honour; to you on the shore, with sea-blue fillets,
and to the Zephyrs and Glaucus a bull, and to Thetis a heifer,
Ancaeus brings down. No other was surer than he
to break the fat necks with the death-bringing axe.
Three times pouring the bowls in libation to the father of the sea,
thus the son of Aeson speaks: 'O you who shake the foaming
realms with your nod, and embrace all lands with your brine,
grant pardon. I know that I, one out of all peoples,
attempt forbidden ways and earn the storm:
but I am not borne of my own will, nor is it my mind now
to pile up mountains, or to demand the thunderbolt from high Olympus.
Let not the prayers of Pelias draw you: he devised the harsh
commands, and the Colchians, against me and the grief of my own:
him only . . . . . . with waves not indignant
receive this head and the alder pressed down by kings.'
So speaking, he heaps the flame with rich offering.

When the fire, struggling in the thick entrails, put forth
its crest and climbed the leaping vitals of the bull,
behold, hallowed and wholly the god's along the shores, Mopsus,
monstrous to look upon, whirls his fillet and his hair
rising through the air, and the laurel. A voice was at last returned,
a voice dread to the men; then silence was made for the seer:
'Alas, what do I behold! Roused but now by our daring,
behold, Neptune calls the gods of the sea and a great
council. They urge to rage and to defend the law.
So in your embrace, so the breast of your brother,
Juno, hold; and you, Pallas, do not desert the ship:
now turn aside the threats of your uncle. They have yielded, and have received
the ship upon the sea. Through how many perils of fortune
am I delivered! Why does fair Hylas veil his hair with sudden
reed? Whence on his shoulders an urn, and through his snow-white limbs
sea-blue garments? Whence these wounds upon you, Pollux?
How great the fire from the swollen nostrils of the bulls?
The helmets rise, and from all the furrows spears,
and now, even now, shoulders. What battle around the fleece
do I behold? What woman, dripping with slaughter, cleaves the air
with winged serpents? Whom does she strike with the sword? Wretched one, snatch up the little ones,
son of Aeson! I see the bridal chamber too ablaze.'

For long . . . he terrifies the Minyans and the leader
with riddling words; but against him the Phoebean Idmon,
dreadful to the men neither by pallor nor by any
bristling of hair, full of fate and with Phoebus at peace,
to whom his sire granted by warning to foreknow the gods'
omens, whether he questioned the flames, or the slippery entrails close at hand,
or the air filled with sure-flying birds,
thus sings to his comrades and to Mopsus: 'As much as the augur Apollo
and the first flame teach, I see indeed the work
full of hard toil, but a work which the enduring ship shall conquer all.
Hold firm, great souls, and stretch out
to the sweet embraces of your parents.' Tears fell as he sang,
because he found Argos already closed to himself amid the fires.

Scarcely had he said this, when the Aesonian leader joined
such words: 'Since you behold the counsels of the gods,
O comrades (and how great a hope is given to great undertakings!),
do you too now bring strength and a father's courage.
Not by me is the piety of the Thessalian tyrant to be blamed,
nor his suspected guile: a god commands these things, a god with a favouring omen;
Jupiter himself willed commerce for his world
and to mingle such great labours of men.
Go, men, with me, and prevail in doubtful affairs,
deeds it shall delight to remember, and which shall urge on our descendants.
But this night, comrades, gladly along the shore
lead through with sweet talk and play as it comes.'
Let it be obeyed. The young men sprawl on the soft seaweed,
and the Tirynthian conspicuous on his couch. The servants
snatched the entrails on spits and gave the corn from baskets.

And now Chiron came running down from the topmost peak,
and showed from afar Achilles calling to his father.
When the boy saw Peleus risen at the well-known voices
and stretching out his arms with a mighty stride,
he leapt to him and long hung upon the dear neck.
Neither the cups foaming with strong Bacchus
nor the figures worth gazing on in ancient metal
hold him; he is amazed among the leaders, and drinks in their great talk,
and brings his face close to the Herculean lion.
But glad Peleus snatches kisses from his clinging son,
and looking up to heaven says: 'If you wish Peleus
to run upon a calm wave,' he says, 'and to gain the favouring winds,
preserve, you gods, this head. The rest, Chiron,
give to me. Let the little one marvel at you telling
of trumpets and wars; under you as master let the boy
bear childish weapons and hasten toward our spear.'
Thence to all warmth was added by the wine: to go through the deep
they wish with high heart. The fleece of Phrixus, though absent,
is promised, and Argo to return with golden clusters at the stern.

The sun rushes down, and for the rejoicing Minyans the waves
drew off the whole day. The lights are scattered along the curving
shore, showing the lands to no sailors yet.
Here the Thracian seer draws out the night with his sweet shell,
telling how Phrixus, his temples bound with fillets,
fled the unjust altars, hidden by clouds,
leaving Athamas to Ino's Learchus;
how the golden ram bore the youth upon the pitying
waves, and how Helle sat clinging to its horns.
The Dawn had run seven courses, and the Moon as many
shadows in the sky, and Sestos, seen far off across no sea,
had begun to part from twin Abydos.
Here the daughter of Aeolus, doomed to abide through all time,
deserts him—alas, in vain snatched from her cruel stepmother.
She indeed, with weary palms, reaches far for the wet
fleece, but the wave drags the garments, soaked
with their pressing weight, and her hands slip from the smooth gold.
What grief was yours, Phrixus, when, driven by the swift surge,
you looked back at the wretched maiden's crying face
and her last hands and her hair scattered across the seas.

And now there was a limit to wine and play, and laid upon
the couches of rest they fell silent; alone of them all, stretched out in order,
impatient of sleep, the leader remains. Him heavy Aeson
and Alcimede, wakeful alike, watch and hold,
their eyes full. To them Jason offers the words
of calm speech, and soothes their troubled hearts.
Soon, when their eyes, overcome by heavy sleep, had closed,
the gleaming guardian of the crowned keel
seemed to press the leader with these words: 'You see the Dodonian oak,
the handmaid of Chaonian Jove. With you I enter the waters,
nor could Saturnia tear me from the prophetic woods
except by the promise of heaven.
The time is here; come, break off delay; and while over the whole sea
we run, if the doubtful sky should draw on clouds,
even now put away fear, trusting in the gods above and in me.'
She had spoken. He, trembling, though the gods' omen was glad,
leapt from his bed. At once Tithonia, kindly, brought before him
all the Minyans, rippling the sea with the new sun of Phoebus.
They scatter to the benches: some loose the yards
from the high mast, others on the marble surface
try out the oars beforehand; from the high prow Argus gathers the rope.

The mothers' groans increase, and the fathers' brave
hearts grow faint; weeping, they cling in long embraces.
Yet the voice of Alcimede rises above all the lamentation.
As much as she rages with womanly wailings,
so much as the war-trumpet of Mars drowns the Idaean boxwood,
she speaks also these words: 'Son, about to face unworthy toils,
we are parted; nor was it given me before to compose my mind
to these chances, but I feared wars for you and lands.
Vows must be made to other gods. If the fates bring you
back to me, if the sea is appeasable to trembling mothers,
I can indeed endure the daylight and the long fear.
But if Fortune prepares otherwise, pity your parents,
kind Death, while there is fear and not yet grief. Ah me, the Colchians—
why did I, and the fleece of carried-off Phrixus, ever dread them?
What days already in my mind, what cruel sleepless nights with cares
I foresee! How often, at the hoarse beating of the shore,
shall I faint, fearing the Scythian sea and sky,
nor, ungrateful, believe my fair weather brings you safety.
Grant me, I pray, your embraces, and leave words to cling
in my ears, and even now press my eyes with your sweet right hand.'
With such words Alcimede mourns; but Aeson, stronger,
lifting up her spirits with words: 'O if I had the blood
I had, as great, when this hand subdued Pholus
threatening with no lighter mixing-bowl of gold,
first upon the bronze-clad ship would I have set my arms
and rejoiced to raise the vessel with the struck oar.
But my country's prayers prevailed, and the vows
heard by the great gods: I see so many kings upon our sea,
and you as their leader. Such, such men was I wont to lead
and to follow. Now that day (may Jupiter grant it, I pray),
that day remains, when victor over the Scythian king and the sea
I shall receive you, your shoulders blazing with the fleece you have seized,
and yield my own deeds to your youth.'
So he speaks. The other supported on his breast the mother
fallen, and received the old man on his great neck.

And now was the end. The third trumpet with its sad signal
had loosed the embraces that held back the West Wind and the ship.
The men each give their names to an oar, give their names to the benches.
Here Telamon holds the leftward sea, higher there
Alcides takes another part, the rest of the company
is divided: swift Asterion, whom as he fell from his mother
his father Cometes of Piresiae cherished by twin streams,
where Enipeus more slowly feels the strength of Apidanus.
Here Talaus strains, and Leodocus presses with his oar
the back of his own brother, men whom noble Argos contributed.
Hence too is sent Idmon, though the birds
forbade him; but it is shameful for a man to have feared the future.
Here too the son of Naubolus rises against the twisted waves,
Iphitus, here Neptunian Euphemus breaks his father's sea,
who holds wave-sounding Psamathe and ever-open
Taenarus, and from the soft shore of Pellene
Deucalion sure with the javelin and at close quarters with the sword,
the noble Amphion, whom Hypso bore alike
and could not, nor wished to, learn to tell their like faces apart.
Then strong Clymenus with battered breast plies the oar,
and his brother Iphiclus draws the ship, and with savage torch
soon to drive the Danaans upon your rocks, Caphereus,
Nauplius, and Oileus who shall groan at the bolt
not hurled by Jove, his son hissing through the Euboean waves,
and Cepheus, who at the Tegean threshold helped
the son of Amphitryon as he sweated under the weight of the Erymanthian
monster, and Amphidamas (but his brother, fuller of deeds,
chose with Ancaeus rather to touch the fleece of Phrixus),
and Eurytion, his neck covered with the saved hair,
whom his father shall shear when he returns to the Aonian altars.
You too, Nestor, the fame of the Thessalian ship snatches into the seas,
who one day at the Mycenaean sails shall marvel
at the white waters and a thousand pressing helmsmen.
Here is the seer, and the not-vain pledge of his father Phoebus,
Mopsus, around whose purple buskin
a white robe flows, striking his lowest feet, and on his filleted brow
a helmet, and at its peak the Penean laurel.
Moreover from the Herculean rank rises Tydeus
and the son of Neleus, Periclymenus, whom little Methone
. . . light Elis in horses, and Aulon facing the waves,
saw breaking the opposing faces with the gauntlet.—

You too, son of Poeas, with your oar seek the Colchians of Phrixus,
fated to see Lemnos twice, now glorious for your father's
spear, one day to wield the Herculean arrows.
Next to him Butes, rich from the Actaean shores;
for he shuts in countless bees and, proud, darkens
the day with a long cloud, while he opens the cells full
of nectar and sends his kings forth to sweet Hymettus.
You follow, Phalerus, and bear your own mishaps
graven on your arms; for slipping from the spreading tree
the serpent encircled you, little, four times with its burning back:
your anxious father stands far off, bending his doubtful bow.
You too bear arms graven with other terrors, Eribotes . . .
nor was Peleus lacking, trusting in his bride a goddess
and in his bride's father, and your spear gleams from the high prow,
son of Aeacus: so much higher than the other spears was it,
as it had surpassed the Pelian rowans on the summit.
The son of Actor too leaves his son in Chiron's cave,
that as a comrade he may study together with dear Achilles
the strings of the lyre, and together as a boy may launch the light spears,
may learn as a rider to mount the back of the gentle master,
and Phlias, whose descent—as fame, not deceived—is from Lyaeus,
his father's hair flowing from his head.
Nor does his mother fear to commit Ancaeus to the deep,
whom she bore to the king of the sea. No less untroubled
upon the waters is Erginus borne, the offspring of Neptune,
who knows the snares of the sea, the stars of the bright night,
and whom Aeolus marks out from his closed caves,
who would not fear if the ship's command, if heaven itself
were handed over by Tiphys, his face wearied with the constant Bear.
Swift the Laconian bears the rough straps with wounding
lead, that at least into the empty winds he may fling
his arms, and the Pagasaean ship may watch the Oebalian
nursling celebrating the shores in untroubled sport.
And Castor, better at curbing mouths with the Thessalian rein,
while he sought a bearer for fearful Helle,
let Cyllarus grow fat on the Amyclaean grass.
On them alike trembles the fiery purple, dyed
with Taenarian crimson, the work their mother on a double web
drew, a thing to behold; twice she had wrought Taygetus
and its leafy woods, twice she had poured Eurotas in soft gold;
and each man's own steed bears him on the snowy thread,
and from the breast of both flies the swan of their father.
But for you the brooch has now loosed the gathered garments
and shown your strong shoulders and the breadth of your proud
breast, equal, Meleager, to the Herculean arms.
Hence a numerous band, the Cyllenian offspring: sure
is Aethalides to gather sudden arrows as the string returns;
you, Eurytus, are good to go through the midst of the foe with the sword;
nor, by your father's craft, ignoble to the Minyans,
Echion, who renders the leader's messages to the peoples.
But not by your arms, Iphis, will Argo return:
alas, swiftly the sad Scythian sand shall leave you,
and shall mourn the idle oar at your bench.
You too the Pheraean fields give, fortunate in so great
a herdsman, Admetus; for in your fields the Delian
made amends, because with thankless bow he had laid Steropes low.
Ah, how often did his sister, meeting the servant in the well-known woods,
weep, when he sought the cool of the Ossaean oak
and was wasting his wretched locks in the rich Boebeis.
Canthus rises at the benches and turns Nereus with his oar,
whom a barbarian spear shall roll in Aeaean dust;
but meanwhile the glory of the bright shield lies beside him,
which his father Abas bore: through the wave the golden
covering cleaves the Euripus, fleeing the Chalcidian sands,
and you rise, Neptune, in the midst, wheeling the high reins
of the half-beast wolves, from the oyster-bearing Geraestus.
But for you, Polyphemus, brought back in your Palladian pine,
it remains before the city to find the relics
of your burning father, the rites long delayed by his servants,
should you come. With shorter oar Idas now seeks the blue
and takes his place, and last of all sits far off at his bench.
But his brother Lynceus is preserved for great uses,
whom Arene bore, who can pierce the earth
and catch with his far-darting sight even silent Styx.
From the midst of the waves he shall give lands to the helmsman
and shall give stars to the ship, and when Jupiter has lost
the heaven in shadow, Lynceus alone shall pass through the clouds.
Moreover the offspring of Cecropian Orithyia is free,
that Zetes and his brother may temper the quivering ropes.
Nor indeed is Odrysian Orpheus spent at the benches,
nor subdues the sea with the oar, but with song teaches
the oars to move, lest everywhere they fight on the surface of the flood.
The son of Aeson gives the sea and the toils of the young men
also to Iphiclus, whom Phylace had sent, worn with age,
no longer for a share in the work, but that he might hand on keen warnings
and the men who would fire the youths with the praises of their great forefathers.
Argus, your care is for your own ship; the walls of Thespiae
give you, skilled by Pallas' gift; yours is the task, lest in any
part the ship draw the silent sea and, split by the wave,
you bind up the wounds with pitch or with soft wax.
Ever-wakeful Tiphys hung upon the Arcadian star,
the son of Hagnias, fortunate, who gave the use of the sluggish
stars and to hold a heavenly course over the seas with the sky as guide.

Behold, through the swift shortcut of the sloping mountain
the eager leader, glad of the trick, recognizes Acastus,
bristling with javelins and flashing with the light of his shield.
When he had carried himself through the shields and the men of the ship's midst,
the son of Aeson cut the mooring-ropes with burning
iron; not otherwise than when the swift hunter flees the glades
and the ravaged lairs, and drives on the horse fearful
for its master, pressing to his breast the tender tigers,
which by cunning he has snatched in his terror, while the savage
mother hunts on Amanus opposite for the cubs she has left.
The ship, driven forth, goes alike; the mothers stand on the shore
and follow with their eyes the bright sails and the shields of the men
struck by the sun, until now the sea, higher than the masts,
and the boundless air, took the ship from those who watched.

Then from his starry citadel the father, beholding the fairest
beginnings of the Greeks, and the great mass of the work
rising up, rejoices; for he does not approve the idleness of his father's reign.
All the gods rejoice as one, and the Fates see the times
coming upon the world for them, and the ways of the waters growing.
But not without alarm at his son's peril, the father,
the Sun, pours forth from his breast such words:
'Highest sire, for whom our daylight, as the years revolve,
accomplishes and renews so many changes, is this your will?
And does the Greek ship now go upon the waves with you as guide
and with favouring nod? Or is it right for me to break off deserved complaints?
Fearing this, and lest there be any envious hand against my son,
I chose not the wealth of the middle earth, nor the wicked
fields of a rich region (let Teucer hold the most fruitful,
and the Libyan, and the house of your Pelops): the harsh fields
I press, bound with savage frost, and we have settled by frozen rivers.
He would yield even these and bear himself off without honour
yet farther, but stiff with cloud and ignorant of things
the zone stands above, and already beats back our fires.
What does the monstrous region, what does barbarous Phasis
with any rivers, what does my offspring offer to alien peoples?
What have the Minyans deserved to complain of? Does he take the Greek
fleece by force? Nay, he refused of his own will to join his troops to fleeing
Phrixus, nor came to the altars of Ino,
but, keeping the man by a share of his rule and by his daughter's
marriage, he sees now grandsons of Greek stock,
and calls them sons-in-law, and lands joined to himself by blood.
Turn aside the ship and the upheavals, father, nor with our wound
open the seas to the men: enough does the wood of the Po,
witness of old grief, and the sisters weeping at the sight of their father.'

At these words he who sees the fleece, given as a gift, fixed for the War-god,
roars and shakes his head, and Pallas tried the contrary,
and Saturnia groaned at the complaints of both.
Then the father: 'These ancient things, established for us, go on
in their order, each fixed from the first beginning of the world
and from its course; for there was no blood of mine in any lands
when I appointed the fates, and the power of justice came to me
hence, when I was building up varied kings through the ages.
And I shall recall the decrees of my own cares:
long since a region, which descends to the sea of the maiden Helle
and as far as the Tanais from the boundless East,
flows with horses and flowers with men, nor against it
has any band dared to lift equal courage and win a name
in wars; so the fates ordained, so I myself cherished the places.
But the final day hastens, and we leave Asia tottering,
and the Greeks demand of me now their own times.
Thence my oaks and tripods and the souls of their fathers
sent this band to the sea. A way is made through the waters
and through the storms, Bellona, for you. Nor does the fleece alone
await its outraging, and nearer is that grief from the snatched
maiden, but no resolve is more firmly fixed in my mind:
for a shepherd shall come from Phrygian Ida,
who shall bring like groans and wraths and mutual gifts
to the Greeks. What wars then, poured forth from the fleet of suitors,
how many winters at Troy with Mycenae weeping,
how many chiefs and sons of gods, what bulwarks shall you see
fall, and Asia yield to the great fates.
Hence from the end of the Danaans it is settled, and I shall cherish other
nations soon. Let the mountains and woods and lakes lie open,
and all the barriers of the sea; let hope and fear be for all.
I myself, the arbiter, by moving the places and earthly heights,
shall make trial, what realms, longest of all for the peoples,
I would wish, and where, assured, I may leave the reins I have given.'
Then he turns his eyes back to the Aegean blue, to the Herculean
might, and gazing on the race of Leda, thus he speaks:
'Reach for the stars, men: my royal house first laid upon the world,
after the wars of fierce Iapetus and the toils of Phlegra,
a hard journey for you and a grievous one of heaven.
So, behold, my Liber, so, the circuit of the world performed,
and Apollo, having tried the lands, returned.'
He spoke, and through the void he aimed a torch flaming
the clouds with a mighty furrow, which, the ship near,
parted into a forked path and sought the brothers,
the sons of Tyndareus, and gently in the midst of their brows
stayed at once upon both, and harmlessly pours a purple
light, one day to be implored by wretched sailors.

Meanwhile savage Boreas, having watched from his Pangaean
height the sails let loose upon the mid-deep,
straightway, roused, makes for Aeolia and the Tyrrhenian
caves. All the grove groans beneath the god's swift wings,
the corn is laid low, and the black sea is stirred beneath the flier.
On the Trinacrian sea, and on the side of receding Pelorus,
stands a rock dreadful to the straits: as high as it rises into the air
with its masses, so far it is sent down beneath the infernal waves.
Nor is another land seen near it, less in crags or caves.
That one Acamas inhabits and naked Pyragmon,
these the storm-clouds and winds hold as their homes, and the shipwrecking
tempest. Hence to the lands and the broad deep
there is a way, hence once they were wont to confound the pole
and the unhappy strait (for not yet was Aeolus then
their ruler, when the stranger Ocean broke through Calpe
from Libya, when, weeping, Oenotria was losing its Sicilian
borders, and the waves were entering amid the mountains),
until from the air the Almighty thundered upon the frightened
winds, and gave them a king, whom the savage host
was bidden to fear: scarcely with the mountain's steel and the rocks
heaped on walls does he master the East winds. When now he cannot
hold back the roaring mouths, the king himself willingly
breaks open the entrances and bars, and calms the wild murmurs at the opened gate.
Boreas as messenger drives him from his lofty throne:
'What an outrage, Aeolus, I have seen from the Pangaean height,'
he says, 'the Greek youth has contrived a new mass with iron
and goes on, rejoicing, and tames the seas with a vast sail,
nor have I freedom to lift the straits from their lowest sands,
such as I was, not yet shut in chains and prison.
Hence their spirit and the confidence of the men in the built ship,
because they see Boreas under a king. Grant me to sink the Greeks
and their mad ship: my own pledges touch me nothing;
only check the threats of men, while close by the Thessalian
shores no other lands have yet seen these sails.'

He had spoken. But within all the winds roar and demand the seas.
Then the son of Hippotes struck the strong gate
with a whirled blast. Glad from their prison the Thracian
horses pour forth, and the Zephyr, and the Notus, his wings
the colour of night, with the brood of the storm-clouds, and the East wind
bristling with squalls and yellow in his head with much sand;
they brought on the storm, and with hoarse drag to the shores
with one mind they bear the curving seas, nor stir the realms
of the trident alone: alike the fiery air rushes down
with thunder, and night presses all things with a pitch-black sky.
The oars are struck from the hands, and the ship, its forehead turned
aslant, takes the resounding blows on its side;
above the trembling mast a sudden whirlwind snatches
the flying sails. What dread then for the trembling Minyans,
when the pitch-black poles flashed, and before the fearful
ship the flickering fires fell, and the yardarm
bent down with its left horn lifted the gaping wave!
Not knowing, they think the storm and the loosed winds
do not rise, but that the sea is thus by nature. Then with sad murmur:
'This it was to defile the forbidden waves with our cables,
which our fathers feared. Scarcely had we loosed the ship from the shore,
and with how great a roar did the Aegean lift itself.
Is it on this sea that the Cyanean cliffs run together?
Or does a sadder sea remain for the wretched? Leave, you lands,
the hope of the deep, and set apart again the sacred floods.'
These things they repeat, weeping to meet a coward's death.
The great-souled son of Amphitryon looks at his quiver
and his useless club; others, terrified, mingle their last
words and join hands and weary their faces,
wholly in the wretched spectacle, when at once the alder
loosens and the ship swallows the sea with a vast gulf.
Now here, now there the East wind, twisting it, lashes it,
now hissing the Notus bears it off with the Zephyrs; on every side
the waters boil, when suddenly Neptune with his three-pronged spear
lifted his sea-blue head from the depths. 'Let Pallas
and my sister have stolen this ship from me,' he says, 'soothing
my breast with their weeping; let the Pharian and Tyrian keels come
and think themselves permitted. How often soon shall I see the sails
snatched by the south winds, and the waves full of evil cries.
Not my Orion nor the Taurus savage with the Pleiad
is the cause of new death. To wretched nations you, Argo,
prepare their fates, nor now deservedly, Tiphys, shall any parent
wish you a quiet Elysium and the shades of the pious.'
This he says, and the father sets the sea and the troubled
shores back in place, and drives off the south winds, which a blue terror
and a heavy wave with wet bosom, and the rain following far behind,
make together for the Aeolian gate over the sea.
The day flashed forth unbarred, and the rainbow unloosed
the sky, and the clouds returned to the topmost mountains.
Now the ship stands out on calm waters, which from the lowest deep
both Thetis and Nereus, the great father-in-law, raise with their mighty arms.
So the leader veils his shoulders with the sacred robe
and takes the Aesonian bowl, which Salmoneus, glad of the gift,
had left in hospitality, and had repaid the quivers with gold—
not yet that madman who would fashion with a four-cleft beam
the weapons of high Jove, and, a rival, against him as he rushed on
would burn either Athos or Rhodope or the high groves of mournful Pisa,
and himself burn the wretched fields of Elis.
With this he pours libation of liquid to the sea, and thus begins:
'Gods, to whom belongs the rule of the waters and the sounding
tempest, and a palace deep within equal to great heaven,
and you, father, who drew the sea and the two-formed gods by lot,
whether this night was chance or the turning of the sky,
that, as the work of the gods above, so this too may shine, and the deep
has its turn to be lifted in turn, or whether the new sight of an unknown ship
and of arms and men drove you to rise into fierce wraths,
let me have atoned enough, and may your divinity, ruler,
now be kinder to me. Grant me to restore to the lands
these lives, and to embrace the threshold of my homeland's gate.
Then in whatever place richest honour feeds your deserved
altars, wherever, dread with wheels and horses,
you stand, father, and on either side mighty Triton holds the flowing
reins, so great will I found you through our cities.'
He had said these things. A shout arises, and the right hands follow
the leader's words. So when great wrath of the gods has fallen
upon the stalls and the harvests, and Sirius, ravager of the Calabrian field,
the anxious band of countrymen gathers into the ancient
grove, and the priest dictates pious vows to the wretched.
But behold, they see the Zephyrs descend with a soft glide;
the hollow pine flies with reins let loose,
and cleaves the brine and spews foam from the three-pronged bronze:
Tiphys steers, and the silent attendants sit at his commands;
just as around the throne of highest Jove all things
lie ready, prepared for the god, the winds and rains and snows
and lightnings and thunders and the rivers still in their springs.

But a sudden fear, keener than every care, shakes the leader,
and a mind foreboding evil, because, having attacked the king's
offspring and cruelly carried off Acastus by guile,
he had left the rest naked to death, and in the midst of the crime
abandoned the father, and walled him round with no defending arms,
himself far off now, holding safety; for surely all the fury
will rush upon him. Nor does he fear in vain, nor tremble at the future.

Fierce Pelias rages, and from his high peak sees the hostile
sails, nor where, burning, he may pour himself out.
Nothing avails his spirit, nothing his realms; he roars, his cohort
shut in by the barrier of the sea, and the brine flashes with weapons and torches.
Not otherwise than when winged Daedalus leapt forth
from the bronze-sounding shore, and beside him his comrade with shorter wings,
a new cloud leaving their homes, the Minoan band
roared in vain and is wearied with the empty sight,
and every horseman returns to Gortyn with full quivers.
Moreover in the chambers and at the very threshold of Acastus
the youth, poured upon the ground, presses with his mouth
the footsteps and the empty traces, and gathering the tracks with scattered hair:
'You too now, perhaps, the image of your mournful father,
my son,' he says, 'and the sighs of our grief come upon you,
and now you see the snares and round about the perils of savage death
a thousandfold. Where, unhappy one, on what shores shall I pursue you?
Not to the Scythian halls nor to the mouths of Pontus
does that cruel man hold his way, but, captured by love of false praise,
he now tears you, boy, to the torments of our old age.
Or if the seas were passable to high ships,
would I not myself have chosen the youths and the fleet?
O house, O household gods, sons in vain.'
He spoke, and at once terrible with frenzy and threatening wrath:
'Here too are your wounds, robber,
here are tears and a dear parent.' At the same time through the high halls
he comes and goes, roaring, and turns over the harshest of things:
as when Thyoneus turned his savage horns against the deserving
Bistonians, and Haemus, unhappy, with a thousand frenzies,
and now the high groves of Rhodope groan, such, hurried along the long
porticoes, his wife and his sons fled from Lycurgus.

Then to Tartarean Jove and the Stygian shades
Alcimede was bringing the sacred rites, anxious above all for so great a son,
in case from the roused shades she might foreknow something better.
And the wife brings Aeson himself, equal in cares and pressing such
fears in his heart, yet willing, for the rite.
In the trenches is blood, and the lavish honour of opened
Phlegethon stands stagnant, and the aged Thessalian woman calls
with savage tumult the lifeless ancestors, and the grandson of great
Pleione. And now to the songs the thin faces
she had brought forth, and, looking sadly on her son and her son's wife,
such things, the blood once tasted, Cretheus unfolded:
'Put away fear: he flies upon the sea, and the nearer he draws,
the more and more does Aea marvel at the prodigies of the gods,
and the oracles shake the fierce Colchians.
Alas, with what fates he advances, what dread to the nations
he goes on. Soon, proud with Scythian spoils and brides,
he will come; I myself could wish then to break the heavy earth.
But for you the king prepares a sad and unholy thing, and troubled
brother's arms, and conceives the savage fires of his wraths.
Why do you not snatch your life from here and swiftly flee your servant limbs?
Go, you are mine; already the pious throng of the silent calls you
to the groves, and your father Aeolus, flitting in the secret fields.'

Meanwhile the mourning house shuddered at the servants' supreme
cry, and the crash spreads through the walls that the king
rouses a thousand hands and now gives orders to those summoned.
The priestess flings down the blazing altars and the robe and the grove,
and Aeson, afraid, looks round at the sudden things,
what to do. As a lion, having hesitated long in the close
mass of men, has pressed his cheeks and his eyes with his jaws,
so cares came over the leader, whether to seize the unwarlike
iron and the gear of his first age, an old man now,
or to sharpen the fathers and the changeable crowd of the realm.
Against him the band poured out, and his wife clinging to his breast,
'Me too,' she says, 'whatever chance approaches, as companion
you shall receive, nor shall I drag out my fate and see my son
without you, having been patient enough of the sky, when first over the deep
he gave his sails, I who could bear so great a grief.'
Such things through tears. And now Aeson looks round,
by what end he may forestall the threats, what fate he may seize
worthy enough: to demand great deaths for his son and house
and the line of Aeolus and the wars that have been fought.
There is also before his eyes another offspring, raw in years,
whom he would wish to learn great spirit and brave deeds,
and one day to remember his father's death.
Therefore he renews the sacred rites. Beneath the night of an old cypress
a bull stood still, foul and pale with much rust,
with sea-blue fillets through its horns
and a brow rough with the foliage of the yew; itself sick, panting,
impatient of the place and terrified at the shade it saw.
This one, after the custom of the unspeakable race, the Thessalian
woman had kept as chief for the late uses of Dis:
. . . when she appeases the threefold mistress and entreats
with her last fire the Stygian homes, even now driving the song
backward to be appeasable; for not before does the black
ferryman carry off the light shades, and they stand bound at the first jaws of Orcus.
When she saw this one survive in time for the terrifying
rites, she resolved on death, and speaks his last words
himself, touching with his hand the horns of the doomed bull:
'You, to whom belongs the rule of Jove and the not-sluggish
journey of light accomplished, names known to me in councils, known in wars,
the great names of mighty grandsons, hallowed by fame;
and you, parent, called up from the shades, that you might see
our death and might endure, forgetting the gods above, our griefs,
grant me the way to a peaceful seat, and let the victim sent before
reconcile me to your places. You, virgin who announce the guilty
to Jove, who look upon the lands with equal eyes,
and you avenging goddesses, and Right, and the aged
parent of the Furies, Punishment, come to the deserving king's house
and bring savage torches. Let a hallowed terror seize his fierce
heart; nor let him think his son's grievous arms
and ship alone will come: let him turn over in his mind fleets and Pontic
standards and kings indignant at the violated shore,
and ever in fear let him run down to the waves,
stirring the sand; let late death close his way and the tried
escapes, and be unable to outrun our curses,
but let him behold the men now, even now returning, and the journey
flashing with gold. I shall stand exulting and against
his face and hands shall I bear my own. Then, if there remains for you
any unattempted and secret crime, and as yet untold lots of death,
give to my deceitful old age shameful
destruction and dishonourable deaths. Not by Mars nor by arms
nor by my son, I pray, let that man ever be deemed worthy
to fall by the sword; let some faithful band, some dear hand of his own
tear and rend the old man, nor cover his limbs with a tomb.
Let our blood take these atonements from the king,
and, alas, all the nations he has sent upon the seas.'—
The greatest of the Furies herself, with heavy right hand, touched
the cups smoking with black gore;
they eagerly drank the blood received in the bowls.

A crash arises; in through the doors burst those who bore the savage
commands and the swords drawn at the royal orders.
Now in the midst of death they behold the old folk, their eyes
filling with death, and vomiting back the gore through their streaming robes;
and at the very threshold, raw in the order of things,
you, boy, pale at the death of your parents you have seen,
they tear away and add to your own. Far off Aeson shuddered,
departing, and bore beneath the clouds a remembering shade.

Beneath our axis, and cut off from the upper world,
sits the hall of the Tartarean father, not to be approached
by the falling pole, should Chaos roll the conquered mass
and lie with its vast maw, which could consume the matter
wearied by its weight and the falling, sinking world.
Here are twin eternal gates, of which one, by harsh
law ever open, receives peoples and kings;
but to try the other is forbidden, and to go against it:
rarely and of its own will it opens, when at times a leader
bearing well-known wounds upon his breast, with helmets and wheels set before,
or one whose home or pursuit was to drive off mortal cares,
honoured faith, fear far off and desire unknown,
or a priest comes in fillets and in chaste raiment.
All these the offspring of Atlas, gentle on his feet
and shaking his torch, leads on. The way shines wide
with the god's fire, until they come to the woods and the pleasant places
of the pious and the fields, where the sun and through the whole
year the sunny day endures, and dances and choruses of men
and songs, and those for whom there is now no desire among peoples.
Into these seats and eternal walls the father leads
his son and his son's wife. Then how great a punishment at the left
gate awaits Pelias, at what threshold he shows.
They marvel at such great noises and the rushing throng
and the places and the infernal honours of kindly virtue.
4. Gaius Valerius Flaccus, Argonautica, Book Four.

And these things the father of the gods no longer bore
with kindly eyes; and pitying his son's faithful love
he sternly rebukes the trembling Juno in burning wrath:

'See how new joys now rise within your silent breast:
helpless on lonely shores the Tirynthian rages on,
while the forgetful Minyae, careless of their abandoned comrade,
hold the deep. So Juno cherishes the Aesonian captain,
anxious in her cares; so she furnishes him with arms and allies.
Already with what wars I see her wavering and afraid
of the Scythian people's might, with what great dread she quakes!
I forbid you to assail me with prayers, with tears,
or with a suppliant hand; firm is my power over things.
Go, rouse the Furies and Venus; the wicked maiden shall pay
the penalty, nor shall we leave Aeetes' groans unavenged.'

He spoke, and dew fragrant with secret nectar,
which holds deep rest and the power of liquid sleep,
he brought, and touched the temples of his wandering son.
He, his eyes growing heavy, bearing always Hylas' name
upon his echoing lips, since no god's power could prevail,
sinks down. At last peace was restored to the weary woods,
and the rivers, and the breezes heard upon the empty hills.

Behold, the boy seemed to lift himself from the topmost wave
amid the saffron leaves, by the cruel Nymph's gift,
and standing above that dear head to utter words like these:
'Why, father, do you waste the hours in vain laments?
This grove, and now by fate my wicked home, where the Nymph
carries me off by savage Juno's command, into the streams.
Now she grants me access to Jove, the very threshold of heaven,
and joins me in wedlock and the honours of the spring.
O grief, O the sweet quivers we once carried before!
Already your comrades have loosed their cables to glad winds,
after the son of Oeneus drove them on with furies
and unspeakable voice. But with his race and house
he shall atone for this, and your power shall aid his cruel mother.
Rise up, then, and never fail amid hardships; soon to heaven
you shall come, and the stars shall bear you; be always mindful
of love, and let not the image of your dear companion fade.'

As he prayed with such words and delighted in the sight,
the other reaches out and presses on with empty embraces,
and moves in vain the efforts of his failing right hand:
his body is dulled with sleep, mocked by the fleeing shade.
Then with tears, then with his voice he tries to follow, to break out in laments,
when sleep dissolves, and his sad hope dies with the vain act.
As when, by chance, the wave from the edge of a sea-sounding rock
snatches the brood and home of the wretched halcyon,
the grieving mother flies above and laments to the swelling waves,
resolved to follow wherever they bear her, daring and dreading,
struck by the waters she sinks until her home is swallowed by the flood;
she, in her sorrow, gives voice and lifts herself on her wings:
not otherwise is the mournful labour of his sleep. He leaps up, frantic,
and bathes his cheeks with streaming tears. 'I shall go,' he says,
'alone, and you will hold these mountains and deserted wilds,
dear boy, nor will you marvel further at our deeds.'
This said, he retraces his ways and comes out from the valleys,
uncertain what Juno brings, what wrath she makes ready.
And no less he sees his comrades borne far off across the sea
headlong, and is silently ashamed that he could be left behind.

And now he had turned his journey toward the Teucri and the friendly walls
of Troy, seeking again the promises of the Ilian tyrant,
when Latona with sorrowful face, and Diana,
stood before Jove, and Apollo speaks thus in supplication:
'For what other Alcides, to what time now do you defer
the aged Caucasian, great king? Will you grant no end at all
to his sufferings and his punishment? All the race of men
entreats you for him; and now the very mountains, best father,
and the weary ridges with their woods implore you. Enough for you
is the theft of fire and the defended silence of the heavenly table.'

When he had spoken, from the crags, amid the very feeding-grounds
of the dread vulture, even he himself wearies Jove
with his groaning and sorrowful voice, easing the burnt-out
sockets of his eyes scorched by the cruel frosts;
the rivers and the Caucasian rocks redouble the din;
the very bird is stunned by the god's outcries.
Then too Iapetus was heard rising above to the upper heights
from Acheron; the grim Erinys keeps the suppliant far off,
regarding the law of lofty Jove. He, moved by the tears
of the goddesses and by the great honour of Phoebus,
sends swift Iris down on rosy clouds.
'Go,' he says, 'let Alcides defer war upon the Phrygians and on Troy;
now let him snatch the Titan from the dread bird.'
The goddess flies and bears to the hero the parent's commands
to be hastened, and fills him eager with glad encouragements.

Now the Minyae, amid the waves beneath the stars of midnight,
had set their hollow sails in calm course over the flood,
and, remembering, kept turning over thoughts of abandoned Hercules.
But the Thracian priest, from the high stern, soothing his comrades
with the fates of the gods and the troubles of wretched life,
drives away care with his numbers and his healing song;
and when its struck note was taken up by the lyre, grief and wrath
and toil and the sweet thought of his son yield from the breast.

Meanwhile, as now the great stars were sinking, the caverns
of the Titaness sound at the bridling, by the cradle-spring of Ocean;
the Sun, while the golden-haired Hours gird him round,
puts on his many-rayed splendour and the breastplate woven
with twelve signs; the belt that varies for mortals the rippling bow
against the clouds binds it fast.
Then over the lands and the horns of the eastern mountain
he flashed forth and drew the day across the shining waves,
and the Minyae, at the sight of Phoebus, were left by the winds.

The nearest shores of the Bebrycian realm are spread open,
a rich soil, a land not grudging to its hardy bulls.
The king is Amycus; trusting in the king's fate and his power,
they have not girded their homes with walls, nor do they keep
any covenants of law or rights that hold minds at peace.
Like the raging Cyclopes in the Aetnaean caves,
who under the winter night watch the straits, where by cruel winds
some ship may be driven to bring you dread fodder
and wretched feasts, Polyphemus: so on every side, on all
the roads, they look out and run, to drag the bodies they have taken
to their king. He himself, fierce, beyond the sacrificial rock
of the ridge, in the midst of the waters, hurls and drives them
to Neptune his father. But if any guest of fairer form be there,
then he bids them take up arms and meet him in turn
with the gauntlets taken up; this is the fairest lot of a wretched death.
When Neptune felt that the ship had been borne hither
on the flood, and looked out upon his son's last on the shores
and the fields once glad with their lord's contests,
he groaned and unrolled such laments from his breast:
'Unhappy Melie, once snatched beneath my deepest waves,
and not rather then joined to the great Thunderer,
does grim fate so await my offspring of every kind,
from whatever origin? So I felt you of old go on, Jupiter,
when by the arms of an unjust maiden my unhappy Orion
fell, and now fills Chaos. Let neither valour now,
nor trust in us, give you courage, my son;
trust not beyond your father's power.
Now, now other forces and the fates of Jove, mightier
than our blood, prevail; his care for his own is the greater.
And therefore I neither tried to turn this ship aside
with swelling winds nor held it back, nor will there now
be any delay to your death. Press hard, harsh one, the lesser kings.'
Then the father turned his eyes away, and leaving his son
and the sad battles, laved the lands with his bloody tide.

First the captain bids them explore the rivers, the people,
and the shores, and Echion, going out a little way,
finds a young man dragging his groans in a dark valley,
secretly, and mourning the name of a slain friend.
When he saw the man coming toward him, and his temples
shaded after his father's manner with the Parrhasian cap,
and in his hand the useless emblems of the peace-bringing wand,
'Alas, flee,' he says, 'whoever you are, doomed man, with sure step,
while it is given.' The Nonacrian offspring was struck dumb at the sight,
wondering what it might mean. When he sees him warning him to go back
more swiftly, and persisting in the same words,
he seizes him and forces him to tell his comrades what these things are.
The man, stretching out his hand, says, 'This land is no land
of welcome to you, men, no reverence for any rites
fills these hearts; death dwells here, and savage fights upon this shore.
Soon dread Amycus will come, who will command us to take up
the gauntlets, and who beats the clouds with his vast head.
Such a one, believed Neptune's offspring, rages eternally
against those who come, and, lacking equal valour,
sets them like sluggish bulls before the wicked altars of the gods,
that at last he may wash his arms in their wretched brains.
Take counsel, and do not scorn the time still left for flight.
For in vain would any man dare to close with that monster;
and what pleasure would there be to have seen such a thing?'
To this the captain says, 'Do you come as a Bebrycian bearing
a heart at variance with your king (for often the will of the crowd
is better), an enemy, or borne by fate from foreign shores?
And why has Amycus not yet crushed your face with the gauntlet?'
'A name,' he says, 'most sweet to me, and following the name
of Otreus, one with me in heart. He, the glory and glad
renown of his own, no companion to be scorned in your deeds,
when he sought Hesione and the joys of his Phrygian bride,
stood here against Amycus by command, and I joined my hands with his;
but scarcely was he raising his face, when from afar the lightning
right hand struck his brow and scattered and shed
his eyes. Me he never deemed worthy of death or arms,
but rather I am consumed by tears and idle grief.
Yet there is hope, if a messenger has appeared on these shores
by my report, and has reached the ancestral cities of the Mariandyni,
from whence are the man's race and his brother — but may even he rest,
I pray, nor let Lycus increase the slaughter with vain arms.'

When the young men, moved by no fear, receive these words,
and see him persist with so hard a mind,
he bids them follow at his back and join their hurrying steps.
On the farthest shore a huge cavern appeared,
covered over with trees and a threatening ridge,
not such as the gifts of the gods, nor such as draws the fire of heaven,
an unhappy house, trembling with the roar of the deep.
But before the rock, varied terrors: here are the severed
arms of men, snatched by the whirling and dead in the clenched gauntlet,
bones foul with decay, and a most mournful row of heads.
You might look on those for whom, beneath the wound that faced them,
there was now no face nor name; in the midst his own arms,
holy with dread, are set upon the altars of his great father.
Here first the warnings of the host Dymas returned,
and dread, and the image of the absent monster rose upon them,
and silent they all held their eyes upon one another,
until Pollux, fearless, with his starlike face,
'Yet you, whoever you are,' he says, 'this terror of yours
I shall make your own woods soon bear, if only you have blood and limbs.'
In all there was the same spirit, to settle it by brave fight,
and they long for the man and demand to meet him face to face.

Just as one opens a passage for a foaming stream from its very depths
through unknown lands, and soon all the flock, its fear driven off,
follows behind, and now goes before from the midst of the waves.

But far off from the woods the savage giant bore himself
and his herds into the caves. His own throng, watching him,
goes with the silent dread of one secure. Nowhere remain
the marks of a mortal; he is the likeness of a crag that goes
highest on the high mountains and stands alone, far from every ridge.
Thence he flies down raging, nor does he ask first by what road,
nor whither nor whence they have set out, nor of their race,
but thunders forth in such wrath:
'Begin, O young men. For confidence, I believe,
has brought you here to shores you challenge of your own accord,
having heard of them. But if by a wandering of the way, and a mind
not yet knowing the place, this is the house of Neptune; I myself
am Neptune's offspring. Here is my law: to raise the gauntlets
and the opposing arms against me. So the great region of Asia,
and all that lies to the right through the north and the sea on the left,
has visited my hospitality; from this contest all kings return.
Long now the gauntlets have lain idle, and the cold ground
is dry with scattered teeth. Who will join a covenant with me?
For whom does my hand bear the first gifts? Soon for all the same
honour shall come. No flight beneath the earth, no flight through the air.
Neither tears (offer no prayers) nor the gods called upon
move my heart; for other shores Jupiter is king.
I will see to it that no ship can cross the Bebrycian
strait, and that the Symplegades fly over an empty sea.'

Such words he was giving, when at once fierce Jason
and at the same time the sons of Aeacus, and Calydon's foster-son,
and the son of Neleus, and Idas first, names that rise
greatest; but Pollux had already stood with bared breast.
Then dread and chill blood fixed Castor fast.
For he sees no battle before the Elean shores of their father,
nor sounds the Oebalian cheer of the arena, nor the known ridges
of Taygetus, where the victor washes by his native streams,
nor the steed as prize, nor the bull of the sacred sand,
but for reward the shades and the unbarred door of death.
Amycus, eyeing him neither grim of brow nor dreadful in bulk,
scarcely yet scattering the signs of first youth,
goes round him with a smiling face and rages that he has dared,
and rolls his bloodshot eyes with burning furies.
Not otherwise did Typhoeus, when, bearing now the realms of heaven,
now the captured stars, he grieved at Bacchus before the lines,
at Pallas first of the gods, and the maiden's snakes set against him.
So indeed he pursues, and so with rabid muttering terrifies him:
'Whoever you are, unhappy boy, make haste; no longer
shall this grace of your fair brow remain to you, nor will you bear
a face known to your mother. Were you chosen by unjust comrades?
Will you die by Amycus' hand?' Delaying no more,
he thrust forward his huge shoulders and the broad bones of his chest
and his dreadful limbs with their shapeless muscles.
The Minyae fail at the sight, and the son of Tyndareus himself
marvels; the longing for Alcides returns now too late,
and with a vacant eye they scanned the mournful mountains.
But the son of the sea-king then speaks thus:
'Look on these coils too, hardened on raw bulls' hide;
nor do I seek the help of the lot, but put on what gauntlets you can.'

He spoke, and through the late atonement of urging fate
he, not knowing this was the last, gave his hands to his servants
to bind with arms, and the Laconian his too. Bitter hatreds rise
between men unknown before, and with kindled minds
the blood of Jove and the offspring of Neptune are borne to the middle.
On this side and that, silences intent on doubtful prayers,
and father Tartarus at last sends out the praying shades
of the slain through a hollow cloud, to the spectacle of the deserved fight;
the summits of the highest mountain grow dark.
At once the Bebrycian, like a snatching whirlwind from the crag
of rugged Malea, scarcely letting the men raise their faces,
scarcely their arms, drives them headlong in a torrent on every side,
enwrapping them in his rushes, and huge he pursues over all the sand.
But Pollux, watchful in his fear, with breast and arms
now this way and now that, his neck always drawn back,
always on his toes and in the dust of the field's surface,
flung forward, returns. As, on the foaming deep,
when the Pleiad is set, a ship that the trembling care of the master
alone holds fast cuts the mad sea unharmed
while the winds contend, so Pollux, watchful, keeps clear of the blows
and snatches his doubtful head away by Oebalian art.
When at last he had poured out from the clouds the urging wrath
and the heat of the man, little by little, unscathed against the weary one,
he begins to rise and draws the highest gauntlets down with his hands.
That day first saw the limbs of Amycus sick with sweat,
and saw him faltering with parched and gaping mouth,
nor do his own places know the weary king, nor his own
ranks. Both draw breath and lower their arms a little,
as when, on the very field, Gradivus revives the Lapiths
or the Paeonians, and stands silent, his spear planted.
Scarcely had they stood, and lo, again they rush, and far around
their struck backs resound; new force again, new bodies rise.
This man shame, that man hope now bolder against a known foe
spurs on. Their hearts smoke with the frequent blows;
the pathless ridges answer with groaning: as when,
ever wakeful, Aetna marks the craftsmen's hands and the Cyclops
forges the thunderbolts, and the cities clamour with the beaten anvils.
Here the son of Tyndareus flashes out and readies his right hand
and threatens with his right; Bebryx turns here with his eyes
and his weight, thinking it so, but the other snatches at his face
with a swift left. The comrades cry out and the joy gives sudden shouts.
Confounded by the unhoped-for stroke and raging,
the son of Oebalus shrinks back from him while his first wrath thunders out,
himself also frightened and conscious of his great daring.
Helpless, Amycus rages, hurling himself with no measure
and greedy for the man (for he looks back at the Minyae
exulting far off); then, raised on both his gauntlets,
he rushes in. Pollux comes in between these and of his own accord
flies at the grim man's face: yet neither hope was fulfilled,
but both his hands fell upon the breast. The fiercer for this,
lo, again the other drives his arms thoughtlessly through the empty air.
For Pollux feels him bereft of reason . . .
he gives his side, with knees joined, and following the spent thrust
he does not let him recall his step, but confounds and presses
the wavering man, and freely heaps frequent blows
from above on him as he turns away; the head sounds at every wound,
bowed down, and yields to the strokes. Now the temples drip
and the ears are hidden with blood, until at last the heavy right hand
loosens the vital bonds where the neck first joins the limb.
The hero drove the falling man forward,
and standing over him, 'I am Pollux, sent from Amyclae
and born of Jove,' he says; 'this name you shall carry to the wondering
shades: so too you shall be known by a remembering tomb.'

At once flight scatters the Bebryces; there is no love
for the king they have lost; swiftly they make for mountain and wood.
This lot, this hand, at last held back Amycus from his savage daring,
who guarded the places of the Pontus and the relentless force
of his youth, and hoped for the years of his great father.
He lies, that huge terror of men, and covers far and wide
the fields, as if a part of the aged Eryx, or all Athos,
should fall someday; at the mass of him lying there
even the victor himself cannot be satisfied, and holds his face
in long wonder, gazing close. But all the band
of heroes press eagerly with thronging embraces,
and gladly bear his arms and lift his weary hands.
'Hail, true offspring of Jove, true offspring of Jove,' they cry
on every side, 'O Taygetus, to be remembered in the great wrestling-grounds,
and that happy labour of his first master.'
And while they speak these words, they see thin blood
flowing from his starlike brow; nor, frightened by the blood,
did Pollux dry his wounds with the gauntlet turned aside.
Castor wreathes his lofty head with branches and his arms,
and binds his temples with green laurel,
and looking back at the ship, 'To my native shores, I pray,
goddess, bear these leaves, and run the straits with this crown.'
He had spoken. Then they cut the herds with the strong axe,
and, drenched, are laid upon the grassy ground, appeased
by the sacred stream of the placated flood; then with cakes and feasts
they heap the leaves; the choicest backs of the cattle
they set apart for the Laconian. Then through all the time of the feast
he rejoices and exults, now in praise of the man, now in the honouring
song of the bard, doubling the bowl to his victorious father.

And now day and the breezes call, and again they make for
the waters where the Bosporus belches out its rigid streams.
These waves, O Nile, the goddess had not yet crossed
for your peoples, whence these names were given to the sea.
Then the holy bard of Oeagrus' bright blood,
reminded by his mother, tells the chances of the place,
and the wanderings of the daughter of Inachus, and sings to the attentive
of the sea and the exiles measured by the heifer:
'Often the men of old saw Jove descend to earth
and the Argive realms of the Pelasgians, to the alluring fires
of the Iasian maiden. Juno feels his guile, and kindled
with care for the marriage-bed, leaped down from the air;
the Lyrcean land and the caves, conscious of the guilt
discovered, trembled at their mistress. Then in fear the rival
took on the face of the Inachian heifer by the god's own will;
Juno fondles her with stroking and soothes her breast,
holding back her sighs with a beaming face.
Soon she addressed Jove thus: "Give me her whom now the field
of rich Argos feeds, bearing the horns of the early moon,
the untamed cow; give your dear wife this gift.
I myself will choose worthy pastures for the beloved beast
and the choicest springs." With what guile could Jupiter
refuse, or what wiles could he invent? Mistress of her gift,
she straightway joins Argus as guardian; Argus the guardian pleases her,
his eyes that know no sleep over all his head, no otherwise
than if a Lydian girl had stained the webs with sprinkled purple.
Argus bids her go by unknown ways into the crags
and the wilds bristling with monsters, alas, much delaying
and trying prayers and words shut up in her breast.
Then yielding, at last she gave her last kisses to her native bank;
Amymone wept, the Messeid waters wept,
and Hyperia wept, calling her back with outstretched arms.
She, whenever her limbs trembled, weary with wanderings,
or when chill evening now rushed down from the highest heaven,
alas, how often she laid her side on a stone, or where, long
sick with thirst, what pools, what fodder she cropped with her mouth,
how often she shuddered at her white shoulders under the lash.
Nay, even as she meditated leaps from a high peak
and dared to die, swift Argus drove her down into the lowest valleys
and harshly kept her at his master's will,
when suddenly the hollow pipe sounded in the Arcadian manner,
and, hastening his father's command, the Cyllenian winged one
came and played a tune on the gentle reed,
and "Where," he says, "do you go off thus apart? Hark, heed the songs."
Not far off, pursuing Argus, his languid . . .
he marks all the eyes following the sweet drowse,
and in the midst of the songs drives home the swift sickle.
And now, restored to Jove little by little in her ancient form,
Io went through the fields, victress over Juno; and lo,
with torches and coils and a Tartarean howl
she sees Tisiphone: and at the first sight she fixes
her steps, and runs back again into the face of the wretched cow,
remembering by no valley, nor where she may stand upon what peak.
By her wandering she is borne even to the Inachian waters,
how changed, and how much, from the first heifer:
neither father nor the trembling nymphs try to approach.
So again the woods, again she seeks the pathless ways behind her,
as if fleeing the Styx, her beloved self; thence through the cities
of Greece she is dragged, and the rivers steep with their banks,
until, hesitating a little before the deep set before her,
she fell upon it: the waves part, and knowing the future
the deeps in fear give her way; she herself shines far off
with her lofty horns, and holds up her dewlaps above the highest wave.
But the maiden of Erebus flies through the air to rich Memphis,
to forestall her and drive her back as she comes from the Pharian land.
Against her the Nile is at hand, and torrential with all his flood
drives Tisiphone and dashes her on the lowest sands
as she cries on the help of Dis and the powers of the cruel realm.
The scattered torches appear, and the whips flung far,
and the snakes shaken from her broken hair.
Nor meanwhile does the hand of Jove rest. The father thunders,
rising in the high heaven, and confesses his care,
and Juno herself dreads his command. She from afar
watches from the citadel of Pharos, now added to the gods, and now
her hair girded with the asp and made a person with the exulting sistrum.
Hence the men of old spread the Bosporus abroad with the name
of the wandering goddess. May she now favour our labours,
and with sent-down east winds carry our ship through her own straits.'

He had spoken, and the gentle winds stretched the sails.
The next Dawn unwove for the Minyae a night's journey
not in vain; they see all things new, and near at hand
the Thynean shores, bristling with the punishments of prophetic Phineus,
whom the god's harsh lot pressed in his utmost age.
For not only an exile and lacking the light,
but on top of this the Harpies, daughters of Typhoeus, the Thunderer's wrath,
ravage him, and plunder the feast from his very mouth.
Such portents and such penalties for his crime
he endures. One hope is left to the old man, that the fates had once granted
the sons of Aquilo to drive off the savage plague.
So when Phineus now feels the Minyae and the sure
help approaching, he is brought by his staff to the first waves,
and tracks the ship, and lifts up his empty eyes.
Then, breathing a thin breath, 'Hail, O hand long
awaited by me, and known to my prayers,' he says.
'I know both for what gods you are born, and what way bears you
on your bidden course, and so I reckoned the hours of your passage,
gathering each nearest thing — how much Vulcanian Lemnos
detained you, what arms unhappy Cyzicus bore.
I felt also the last fight on the Bebrycian shore,
now nearer, and now soothing my soul with this comfort.
Not now that Phineus is sprung from great Agenor,
nor would I record that Apollo my master has settled
in my breast as prophet; pity rather my present fate.
Nor is it time for me to weep the world wandered through
in diverse chances, the homes lost, or the sweet
light; it is too late, by the wonted fates in their order,
to groan. The Harpies always watch my food,
nowhere is there a place to cheat them, wretched as I am: at once they all
come down like a black cloud in a twisted whirlwind,
and now Celaeno is known to me far off by her wings and her sound;
they tear and sweep away the feast and foul and overturn the cups,
the stench rages, and a most wretched fight arises,
and equal is the hunger between me and the monsters. What all have spurned
and polluted with their hand, and what has slipped from their black claws,
this brings me these delays in the light. Nor is it allowed to break
the fates by death; in cruel want my life is dragged out.
But you, O save me, I pray, if the foretellings of the gods
are not false to me, you set an end to my punishments.
Surely they are here who shall put the monsters to flight, the offspring
of Aquilo, not strangers to me; for I was king of rich Hebrus,
and Cleopatra was once joined to your couch as one with me.'

At the name of the Actaean sister, Calais and Zetes
leap forth, and Zetes first, 'Whom do we behold?' he says.
'Are you that Phineus, famed king of the Odrysian shore?
You, companion of Phoebus, and dear to our parent?
O where now is the glory of your kingdom and your race? How
toil has eaten you away, and old age swift to come with woes.
But come, send up prayers; for our will is yours,
if the gods' wrath does not press you, or if it can be appeased.'
Here Phineus lifted his two palms to the stars,
'And you,' he says, 'wrath of the Thunderer, who now press me hated,
I pray, spare at last my old age;
let there be a measure, and I believe indeed there shall be; for your will,
what is it, young men, without the peace of the gods? Nor believe
that any guilt of savagery, or charges of crimes, are now paid by me:
talkative, I had betrayed the fates, and the mind of Jove, and what hidden
counsels he alone, and what suddenly to come upon the earth, he was preparing,
pitying the race of men; hence this great
plague upon me, and the darkness poured over me in the midst of my words.
Now at last the wrath has yielded, nor by chance from on high,
but the god himself, willing, has brought you to our shores.'
So he speaks, and, the fates now yielding thus, he urged them all
and stirred them with the image of his harsh punishment.
They set up couches and receive him in the midst of the spread tapestries,
and lie about him; at once they watch the seas,
at once the stars, and bid him eat and cast off his cares:
when a sudden trembling seized the wretched one, and the first morsels
fled the old man's pale lips and his hands. Nor was the plague betrayed
before, but in the midst of the feast they saw the birds.
